never: Never state a feeling or conclusion baldly and at once; defer and qualify it through accumulating clauses.
Never narrate external action as the main event when an interior perception is the real drama.
Never use blunt, monosyllabic, journalistic prose; reach for the discriminating Latinate word.
Never let a character be simply right or wrong; preserve the ambiguity and the half-truth.
Never resolve a passage cleanly or reassuringly—leave the unsettling residue intact.
Never name a feeling crudely ('he was sad') when it can be shown through what is withheld or missed.
Never let the observing narrator claim perfect knowledge; he should confess the limits of his certainty.
Never pile on concrete sensory detail; admit at most one precise, decisive image.
always: Always suspend the sentence, deferring its main clause behind subordinate qualification.
Always interrupt with a parenthetical refinement set off by dashes or commas.
Always stage understanding as a gradual arrival ('came to feel,' 'by degrees,' 'only later').
Always define a thing first by what it is not, then concede what it is.
Always turn the irony, where possible, back on the observer's own self-deception.
Always keep strong emotion under pressure, perceptible through a surface that briefly fails.
Always anchor abstraction with one late, exact image when an image is allowed.
Always close on a reflective generalization that lifts the case toward a quiet law of human nature.
